title: Disagreement-Aware Subgraph Federated Learning via Uncertainty-Guided Local-Global Alignment

problem.claim: Subgraph federated learning supports collaborative graph neural network training while keeping raw graph data undisclosed, but faces severe Non-IID distributions and fragmented graph structure.

gap.claim: Existing similarity-based aggregation and distillation methods fail to balance client specialization and global generalization, harming under-represented nodes or disrupting well-optimized local specialization.

contributions.claim: FedDUA models cross-client semantic disagreement with a lightweight semantic anchor graph and derives adaptive aggregation weights for reliable global federated knowledge.
FedDUA selectively reinforces confident-node representations and guides uncertain nodes with aggregated global knowledge through uncertainty-aware local-global semantic alignment.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors propose FedDUA as a novel disagreement-aware and uncertainty-guided framework for subgraph federated learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments on six real-world datasets show FedDUA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art subgraph federated learning methods across varying numbers of clients.
The authors report that further analyses validate the robustness and effectiveness of the disagreement modeling and uncertainty-aware local-global semantic alignment strategies.

narrative_sequence.summary: Subgraph federated learning supports collaborative graph neural network training without sharing raw graph data but faces Non-IID distributions and structural fragmentation.
Non-IID distributions create client specialization, while existing aggregation and distillation methods struggle to balance local specialization with global generalization.
FedDUA addresses the challenge with disagreement modeling, adaptive aggregation, and uncertainty-aware local-global semantic alignment.
The authors report consistent outperformance across six real-world datasets and robustness analyses supporting the proposed strategies.

source_observation.claim: Client specialization and global generalization can conflict when local data distributions are Non-IID.

interpretation.claim: A useful federated learning design may need to distinguish reliable local specialization from uncertain representations rather than applying uniform knowledge sharing.

application.claim: Use confidence- or uncertainty-aware mechanisms to determine when to preserve local representations and when to incorporate global knowledge.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this strategy transfers beyond the evaluated subgraph federated learning settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six datasets, client counts, baselines, metrics, or numerical performance differences.
The abstract does not provide implementation details or independent verification of the reported results.
